FPMC combines persistent user preferences and first-order transitions: s(u,j)=p_uᵀq_j+m_{x_t}ᵀn_j; separate source/target embeddings permit asymmetric transitions. FOSSIL replaces the user vector with normalized history pooling and adds weighted recent items: s(u,j)=b_j+[|H_u\{j}|^(−γ)Σ_{i∈H_u\{j}}P_i+Σ_{k=1}^L(η_k+η_{u,k})P_{x_{t+1−k}}]ᵀQ_j. It shares source/candidate tables across long- and short-term components, but retains distinct P and Q. These equations appear in the [FOSSIL paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.09152), including its discussion of FPMC.

For the proposed SASRec augmentation, assuming t is the last observed position and no subsequent normalization, s_t(j)=h_tᵀE_j+(α/3)Σ_{r=0}²E_{x_{t−r}}ᵀE_j. Thus the added branch is exactly uniform three-item similarity scoring. Unlike FOSSIL’s asymmetric P_iᵀQ_j, tied embeddings impose a symmetric Gram similarity. The contextual h_t already captures sequence-dependent preferences, rather than representing a fixed persistent user vector; [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) explicitly learns which historical actions matter. Interpretation: an established recency mechanism supplied through a direct residual path; additional utility requires validation evidence.

Ablate plain SASRec (α=0), last-item only, three-item mean, previous-two mean excluding the last item, full-prefix mean, and older-prefix mean excluding recent items. Compare uniform versus learned lag weights and tied versus separate source/target embeddings. Shuffling only the three-item branch is mathematically inert; shuffle the encoder input separately to assess order. Match tuning budgets, mask padding, use causal prefixes during training, and compare all variants on the same four-category macro validation HR@10. These controls distinguish last-item similarity, additional recent context, and general history pooling.
